module: D10-14 Industrial Policy／Subsidy／Geopolitical Bottleneck產業政策補貼與地緣瓶頸

sources.use: 2026 evidence on subsidy-driven trade reallocation, spillovers and tariff interaction.
Benefits, fiscal cost, government-failure and retaliation risks.
Industrial-policy interface, subsidy transparency gaps and fragmented-response risk.
Capacity-location policy example where licensing permits operation but not expansion/technology upgrade.

mechanisms: Subsidies/tax credits can change relative cost of capacity location and accelerate strategic-sector investment.
Industrial policy can create second-order demand for local suppliers, infrastructure and equipment when eligibility/local-content rules are binding.
Geopolitical bottlenecks can raise the option value of redundant capacity, inventory and geographic diversification.
falsification: Program authorization or award does not equal usable capacity; construction, equipment, qualification and ramp clocks can be years apart.
A subsidy can intensify overcapacity and price competition, reducing margins even while physical capacity expands.
Benefits can leak abroad through imported equipment/materials or be offset by local labor, power, permitting and compliance constraints.
Retaliation, tariffs or counter-subsidies can offset first-order gains and redirect trade.
WTO/IMF evidence shows industrial policy can create cross-border distortions and welfare losses; 'subsidized sector' is not automatically 'good equity return'.
Geopolitical bottleneck narratives can fade if alternate suppliers, inventories or technology substitution emerge.
